theme: Contend, O LORD, with those who contend with me
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 35. David asks God to defend him against false accusers. Read it as a prayer of someone who has been repaid evil for good.
settingTheScene: Psalm 35 is a psalm of David, and it is one of the longest of his cries against enemies. It uses the language of the courtroom and the battlefield. It likely comes from the years of persecution under Saul, when David was accused unjustly and hunted. In the Bible, such prayers are not about private revenge but about asking God to act as judge and defender.
observation: “Contend, O LORD, with those who contend with me; fight against those who fight against me!” (v. 1).
“Say to my soul, I am your salvation!” (v. 3).
“For without cause they hid their net for me; without cause they dug a pit for my life” (v. 7).
“Then my soul will rejoice in the LORD, exulting in his salvation” (v. 9).
“All my bones shall say, O LORD, who is like you, delivering the poor from him who is too strong for him?” (v. 10).
“They repay me evil for good; my soul is bereft” (v. 12).
“But I, when they were sick, wore sackcloth; I afflicted myself with fasting; I prayed with head bowed on my chest” (vv. 13).
“Then my tongue shall tell of your righteousness and of your praise all the day long” (v. 28).
interpretation:
The psalm opens with the call for God to fight. The language is of a defense attorney and of a soldier. David is asking the Lord to take his side. It is not private vengeance but an appeal to divine justice. He does not take up the sword himself. Instead, he asks God to act. We see this restraint in David’s behavior toward Saul.

At the heart of the request is verse 3: “Say to my soul, I am your salvation!” More than victory over enemies, David wants assurance that God is his. The deepest need in times of attack is to know that God is for us.

The center of the psalm is the contrast between how David treated his enemies and how they treated him. When they were sick, he wore sackcloth and fasted and prayed for them. Now they gather against him and mock. This is the hardest part: being repaid evil for good. “They repay me evil for good; my soul is bereft.” David feels deep grief at the unfairness, and he brings it to God.

This is the kind of pain that Jesus experienced. The psalm’s lines “without cause” and “they hated me without a cause” are quoted by Jesus in John 15:25 as fulfilled in him. He healed, taught, and served, and was repaid with hatred.

The psalm has three cycles, each ending with a vow of praise (verses 9 to 10, 18, and 27 to 28). In each, David moves from lament to anticipated thanksgiving. He ends by saying that his tongue will tell of God’s righteousness all day long. The pattern is a model for prayer in the face of injustice: tell God the truth, ask for his help, and promise to praise.

The imprecatory parts of the psalm, in which David asks for the shame of his enemies, should be read as a request that God’s justice would be done, and not as a license for personal hatred.
connection: Jesus quoted verse 19 in John 15:25: “They hated me without a cause.” He was falsely accused, mocked, and betrayed (Matthew 26:59-61). He answered with love and forgiveness (Luke 23:34). Paul teaches, “Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse” (Romans 12:14). 1 Peter 3:9 says, “Do not repay evil for evil… but on the contrary, bless.”
application:
If someone has repaid your kindness with cruelty, bring it to God in prayer rather than responding in kind.

Ask God to “say to your soul, I am your salvation.” Pause and listen.

Consider how you can pray for an enemy as David did when they were sick.
prayerPrompts: Bring God your hurt about being repaid evil for good.
Ask him to help you bless and not curse.
Thank Jesus for being hated without cause.
